title: The normal heart in five views

items.question: Which is the correct order of the five screening planes, moving towards the fetal head?
options: Upper abdomen, four-chamber, LVOT, RVOT / three-vessel, three-vessel-and-trachea
Four-chamber, upper abdomen, RVOT, LVOT, three-vessel-and-trachea
Upper abdomen, LVOT, four-chamber, three-vessel-and-trachea, RVOT
Four-chamber, LVOT, RVOT, upper abdomen, three-vessel
items.explanation: One transverse sweep from the upper abdomen to the upper mediastinum.

items.question: What is the normal cardiac axis?
options: About 45 degrees to the left, 20 degrees either way
About 20 degrees to the left, 10 degrees either way
About 90 degrees to the left
Midline
items.explanation: 45 degrees plus or minus 20, measured against the front-to-back axis of the chest.

items.question: How much of the chest area does a normal heart occupy?
options: No more than about one third
About one tenth
About two thirds
About one half
items.explanation: Usually no larger than a third of the chest area.

items.question: The fetal heart rate stays at 105 beats per minute throughout the scan in an otherwise well fetus. What next?
options: Timely review by a fetal cardiac specialist
Nothing; this is within the normal range
Repeat the anomaly scan in the third trimester
Record it as transient probe-pressure bradycardia
items.explanation: Normal is 120 to 160. Persistent bradycardia at 110 or below needs specialist evaluation; transient slowing from probe pressure does not persist.

items.question: You can count four chambers. Is the four-chamber view normal?
options: Not yet: the view has specific criteria beyond the count
Yes: four chambers means the view is normal
Yes, provided the heart rate is normal
Only colour Doppler can tell
items.explanation: The four-chamber and three-vessel views need much more than a count of structures.

items.question: In normal situs, where are the great vessels in the upper-abdomen plane?
options: Aorta left of the spine, inferior vena cava right of the spine
Aorta right of the spine, inferior vena cava left of the spine
Both on the left of the spine
Both on the right of the spine
items.explanation: Stomach left; aorta left; vena cava right.

items.question: What must be established before assessing situs?
options: Which side is the fetal left and right
The cardiac axis
The heart rate
The size of the great arteries
items.explanation: Laterality first, from the fetal position in the uterus.

items.question: When is mid-trimester cardiac screening best performed?
options: 18 to 22 weeks
11 to 14 weeks
24 to 28 weeks
After 32 weeks
items.explanation: 18 to 22 weeks is the optimal window.

items.question: How far should you zoom for the cardiac views?
options: Until the heart fills a third to a half of the screen
Until the whole fetus is on screen
Until the heart fills about a tenth of the screen
Zoom does not matter if the frame rate is high
items.explanation: Magnify until the heart fills at least one third to one half of the screen.

items.question: Which group of settings suits a cardiac screen?
options: High frame rate, low persistence, single focal zone, narrow sector
Low frame rate, high persistence, multiple focal zones, wide sector
High frame rate, high persistence, multiple focal zones, wide sector
Low frame rate, low persistence, single focal zone, wide sector
items.explanation: These are usually built into the cardiac preset.

items.question: At 20 weeks the left ventricle looks clearly smaller than the right. How should you treat this?
options: As abnormal until proven otherwise: arrange further examination
As a normal variant at this stage
As an artefact of the beam angle
As normal if the heart rate is regular
items.explanation: Mild disproportion can be a variant in the third trimester, but asymmetry in mid-pregnancy warrants further examination. Causes include coarctation, evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary veins.

items.question: Which structure marks the morphological right ventricle in the four-chamber view?
options: The moderator band near the apex
The smooth wall forming the apex of the heart
The foramen ovale flap
The pulmonary veins
items.explanation: The moderator band identifies the right ventricle; the smooth left ventricle forms the apex.

items.question: The two atrioventricular valves appear to attach to the septum at exactly the same level. What does this suggest?
options: Possible atrioventricular septal defect
A normal crux
Tricuspid regurgitation
A normal third-trimester variant
items.explanation: Normally the tricuspid septal leaflet inserts nearer the apex than the mitral. Abnormal alignment is a key finding in atrioventricular septal defect.

items.question: With the beam running along the ventricular septum, you see a gap near the crux. What is the first thing to do?
options: Re-image with the beam at right angles to the septum
Report a ventricular septal defect
Report an atrioventricular septal defect
Ignore it
items.explanation: A beam parallel to the septum can produce drop-out that mimics a defect near the crux. The septum is best seen perpendicular to the beam.

items.question: What confirms a normal left ventricular outflow tract view?
options: The vessel's front wall is continuous with the septum and the vessel does not divide
The vessel divides into two branches soon after its origin
The vessel runs parallel to the other great artery
The vessel is clearly larger than the other great artery
items.explanation: Septal continuity and no bifurcation identify the aorta leaving the left ventricle.

items.question: How do the two great arteries normally relate as they leave the heart?
options: They cross, the pulmonary artery passing in front almost at a right angle
They run side by side in parallel
The aorta passes in front of the pulmonary artery
They arise from a single common vessel
items.explanation: Normal crossover: the pulmonary artery crosses the ascending aorta at nearly a right angle.

items.question: In the normal three-vessel view, what is the order from fetal left to right?
options: Pulmonary artery, aorta, superior vena cava
Aorta, pulmonary artery, superior vena cava
Superior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery
Pulmonary artery, superior vena cava, aorta
items.explanation: Pulmonary artery (largest, most anterior), aorta, superior vena cava (smallest, most posterior).

items.question: The four-chamber view is normal. Which view is most likely to expose transposition of the great arteries?
options: The outflow-tract and three-vessel views
The upper-abdomen view
A repeat four-chamber view with more zoom
None; it cannot be detected on screening
items.explanation: Transposition can have a normal-looking four-chamber view but is typically abnormal in the three-vessel view.

items.question: What is the normal appearance of the three-vessel-and-trachea view?
options: Both arches to the left of the trachea, meeting in a V
One arch on each side of the trachea
Both arches to the right of the trachea
The arches running parallel without meeting
items.explanation: The ductal and aortic arches both pass left of the trachea and form a V.

items.question: What colour velocity scale suits the heart and great arteries in a mid-trimester screen?
options: About 50 to 70 cm/s
About 5 to 10 cm/s
About 15 to 25 cm/s
About 150 to 200 cm/s
items.explanation: About 50 to 70 cm/s for intracardiac structures and vessels; about 15 to 25 cm/s is for veins.

items.question: You notice occasional skipped beats in an otherwise normal low-risk scan. What is the usual significance?
options: Often benign and self-resolving; refer if frequent or persisting beyond a week or two
Always a sign of structural heart disease
An indication for immediate delivery planning
A sign of heart block
items.explanation: Ectopic beats are the commonest rhythm disturbance and are often benign. Frequent episodes or persistent irregularity need further assessment.

items.question: A thin rim of pericardial fluid, under 2 mm, is seen at 28 weeks. How do you interpret it?
options: A normal finding
A pericardial effusion needing urgent referral
A sign of hydrops
A sign of infection
items.explanation: A small amount of pericardial fluid, 2 mm or less at end-systole, is common in the second and third trimesters and is normal.
